courses.title: 01. Read HTTP and map a web application
courses.summary: Learn requests, responses and trust boundaries. Find unnecessary diagnostic exposure in a fictional shop and write your first evidence-based finding.

lessons.title: Define the experiment
paragraphs: A security test asks whether an application permits an action outside its intended rules. Begin with the asset, actor and allowed action: a visitor may see shop availability, while internal configuration belongs to operators. Test only this lab or a system for which you have explicit authorization and a defined scope. Keep a record of the expected rule before sending a probe.

VoltShop is an in-memory teaching application. Requests run through local handlers, and all accounts, files and services are fictional fixtures. Changing a URL in the lab never contacts that host. The request editor acts like a small HTTP repeater: send one request, inspect it, change one value and compare.
lessons.pitfall: A successful status code alone does not prove a vulnerability. Explain which rule the response violated.

lessons.title: Anatomy of an HTTP exchange
paragraphs: A request has a method, a target path, headers and sometimes a body. GET normally retrieves a representation; PATCH updates selected fields; POST submits an operation. The response has a status, headers and a body. In this lab, headers and bodies are edited as JSON objects, which is a convenience of the editor rather than raw HTTP wire syntax.

Send GET /health and locate status 200, the JSON content type and the service status. Try POST /health: the route exists but does not support that method, so the model returns 405. Requesting /missing returns 404. A route list describes attack surface, but it does not tell you whether each route enforces its rules.
lessons.pitfall: Do not confuse a JSON editor with the exact bytes transmitted by an HTTP client.

lessons.title: Find an information boundary
paragraphs: An operator may need detailed diagnostics, but publishing the same data to visitors exposes internal structure. Compare /health with /debug. The public health response should provide only the information needed to determine availability. The diagnostic fixture reveals an internal service address and a demo configuration marker without a session.

Record the anonymous request and the specific response fields. The fixture contains no usable secret: the demonstrated impact is disclosure of internal structure. Keep this narrow claim separate from an unproven claim about account takeover. Discovering an internal URL may guide another test, but it is not proof that the URL can be reached.
lessons.pitfall: Avoid inflating an internal hostname disclosure into a confirmed credential leak.

lessons.title: Retest and communicate
paragraphs: Enable Disable public debug data and repeat the probe. The diagnostic route should return 404 while GET /health still returns 200. This paired check matters: shutting down the entire application would also block the probe, but would break the intended service. The regression runner tests the control and the normal request using fresh fixtures.

A useful report states the affected route, actor, steps, expected result, observed result, impact and remediation. Use the notebook to explain what you observed, then export the report with the captured exchanges. A report generated by this lab is a learning artifact, not an assessment of the deployed VoltQuest application.
lessons.pitfall: Describe the result of the retest, not merely the fact that a setting was changed.

steps: Load the normal request and send GET /health. Record its 200 response and minimal JSON fields.
Request /debug without a Cookie header. Identify the internal service address in the 200 response.
Enable Disable public debug data. Repeat /debug, expecting 404, then repeat /health, expecting 200.
Run regression checks and write the actor, exposed fields, expected boundary and retest result in your investigation notes.
courses.challenge: Compare GET /missing, POST /health and GET /debug. Explain why only one of the vulnerable responses demonstrates an information disclosure.

practice.prompt: Which part of a request selects GET or POST?
practice.explanation: The method describes the requested operation; it is separate from the path and body.

options.text: The authorized scope and expected rule

practice.explanation: Scope identifies permitted targets and actions; the expected rule makes the result meaningful.

practice.prompt: Which field in /debug supports the demonstrated finding?
practice.explanation: The debug fixture exposes internal structure to a visitor who does not need it.

options.text: The route has an exploitable vulnerability
The request was handled successfully at the HTTP level

questions.explanation: Security impact requires inspecting the operation, data and expected authorization rule.

options.text: GET /health still returns the intended public status

questions.explanation: A remediation should contain the unwanted disclosure while preserving the intended public operation.

questions.prompt: What happens when the lab receives an unfamiliar external destination?

options.text: It cannot contact a real host; only known fixtures can respond
It proxies through the VoltQuest backend

questions.explanation: The model has no network transport or backend execution.

questions.prompt: What is a precise impact statement for this debug fixture?

options.text: All user passwords have been stolen
The host operating system is compromised
An anonymous visitor learns internal application structure

questions.explanation: No real credential or operating-system compromise is demonstrated by this fixture.

questions.prompt: Which report is easiest to reproduce?

options.text: One containing only a screenshot of a red label
One with the exact request, actor, response evidence and retest
One containing only a vulnerability name

questions.explanation: Reproduction needs the inputs and observed outputs as well as the expected rule.

courses.title: 02. Find broken object authorization
courses.summary: Test ownership checks by changing an order id while preserving the same customer session. Learn the difference between authentication and authorization.

lessons.title: Identity is only the starting point
paragraphs: Authentication establishes who is making a request. Authorization decides whether that identity may act on a particular resource. Alice can be correctly logged in and still be forbidden to read Bob’s order. A check that merely requires a session answers the first question without answering the second.

The fixture contains Alice’s order 1001 and Bob’s order 1002. Each record has its own owner field. A customer should read their own record; the administrator may read both. Think of this as a small actor-by-object matrix rather than a single logged-in flag.
lessons.pitfall: A login screen does not protect every object behind it.

lessons.title: Change the reference, keep the actor
paragraphs: Start with Cookie: sid=alice-session and GET /orders/1001. Preserve that header and change only the last path segment to 1002. If Bob’s address comes back, the server has accepted a direct object reference without enforcing the relationship between the session and the record.

The lab uses readable ids so the test is easy to repeat. Random or unguessable ids can make discovery harder but do not replace an ownership check. A leaked link, shared URL or another feature might expose an id even when it is difficult to guess.
lessons.pitfall: Switching to Bob’s session while reading Bob’s order is a permitted operation, not an ownership bypass.

lessons.title: Enforce the relationship at the handler
paragraphs: The handler should load the record and compare order.owner with the trusted session user before returning it. An explicitly permitted administrator can be handled as a separate policy branch. The decision belongs on the server for every relevant operation, including reads, updates and downloads.

Enable Check order ownership and resend the same Alice-to-Bob request. It should return 403. Read order 1001 again and expect 200. The fixture uses 403 to make the failed permission check visible; real applications may use a consistent 404 policy to avoid disclosing whether a protected object exists.
lessons.pitfall: Removing a link from the interface does not stop a request to its underlying route.

lessons.title: Test both directions
paragraphs: A one-sided test can miss a rule that accidentally treats one user specially. Reverse the actors: Bob requesting Alice’s order should fail too. Then remove the cookie and confirm 401. Read both orders as the administrator to confirm that the intended administrative exception still works.

Your report should identify the unauthorized record fields and the missing ownership relationship. Do not claim all database records are exposed from a single order observation. State which ids and roles were exercised, and include both permitted and denied requests after the patch.
lessons.pitfall: A test that checks only the response status can miss protected fields accidentally returned in an error body.

steps: Send /orders/1001 with sid=alice-session and observe Alice’s own record.
Change only the path to /orders/1002. The vulnerable handler returns Bob’s address with status 200.
Enable Check order ownership. The cross-customer request must return 403 while Alice’s own order remains 200.
Run regression checks, reverse the two customers and document which relationship now prevents the disclosure.
courses.challenge: Build a matrix for anonymous, Alice, Bob and administrator access to orders 1001 and 1002. Record the expected and observed status for every cell.

practice.prompt: Alice logs in correctly but reads Bob’s order. What failed?
practice.explanation: Her identity is known, but the requested object is outside her permitted relationship.

practice.prompt: Which value should stay unchanged in the first ownership probe?
practice.explanation: Keeping the actor fixed isolates the effect of changing the object reference.

practice.prompt: Do random ids replace authorization?

options.text: Yes; hard-to-guess ids authorize their holders
No; the server must still check access to the object

practice.explanation: An id can be disclosed elsewhere; it is a reference rather than proof of permission.

questions.prompt: Which comparison is central to the customer ownership policy?

options.text: The customer name against a browser label
order.owner against the authenticated session user
The address length against the URL length

questions.explanation: The trusted identity and the resource owner define the permitted relationship.

questions.prompt: After the patch, what should Alice receive for order 1002 in this lab?

options.text: 200 with the address hidden only by CSS

questions.explanation: The handler denies the read before returning the protected object.

questions.prompt: Why test Bob requesting Alice’s order too?

options.text: To prove every route is secure
To detect an asymmetric or user-specific permission mistake

questions.explanation: An independent reverse test expands the exercised authorization matrix.

questions.prompt: What should the anonymous order request return in this fixture?

options.text: 401 because no valid session was supplied

questions.explanation: Authentication is required before order-specific authorization.

questions.prompt: Which fix survives direct requests outside the UI?

options.text: A server-side ownership check on the handler

questions.explanation: Client presentation changes do not constrain callers of the endpoint.

courses.title: 03. Trust sessions, not client claims
courses.summary: Investigate a forged role header. Trace identity from a fictional session store to an administrator-only operation.

lessons.title: Where a role comes from
paragraphs: The browser can send headers and body fields, but their presence does not make them authoritative. A request containing x-role: admin is a claim made by the caller. The application should obtain the user’s role from a trusted session or a correctly verified identity token and apply its permission policy there.

In this lab, sid values select fixed demonstration sessions. These readable values are deliberate teaching fixtures, not a production session design. Real session identifiers need unpredictability, lifecycle controls and protected transport. None of those properties can be demonstrated by changing the public fixture cookie.
lessons.pitfall: A field named role or admin is not trusted merely because it appears in a header.

lessons.title: Compare legitimate and forged administration
paragraphs: First send GET /admin with sid=admin-session and confirm 200. Then use sid=alice-session without x-role: the route should return 403. Add x-role: admin while keeping Alice’s cookie. The vulnerable handler lets this caller-controlled field override the role stored on the server.

Read the trace to see the effective role and its source. The important difference is not the visible name in the UI; it is the value used in the permission decision. This experiment models a trust mistake at the application boundary, not a cryptographic token-signature attack.
lessons.pitfall: Changing the session to the real demo administrator proves normal access, not impersonation.

lessons.title: Repair the trust decision
paragraphs: Enable Use the server session role and resend the forged header. The same Alice request must now return 403 because the role comes from her server record. The header may still be present in the request, but the policy ignores it. The legitimate administrator should retain access.

An unrecognized sid must never become an authenticated account because an admin-looking field was supplied. Remove or corrupt the session value and test again. The model returns 401 before it reaches the administrator role decision.
lessons.pitfall: A secret-looking custom header is not an authentication mechanism when arbitrary clients can choose its value.

lessons.title: Sessions beyond this model
paragraphs: A complete authentication system also needs secure credential handling, session rotation after privilege changes, expiry, logout invalidation and protections against guessing. Cookie flags such as HttpOnly and Secure address particular browser and transport risks; they do not correct an authorization decision that trusts a caller-supplied role.

Keep the finding focused: a customer session can use a role header to access the admin fixture. Include the normal administrator request, the denied customer request and the forged request. Retest each after the fix so the boundary is visible without claiming that every session-security requirement has been verified.
lessons.pitfall: Fixing this role-source bug does not establish that login, session storage and logout are all secure.

steps: Send GET /admin with sid=admin-session, expecting 200. Switch to sid=alice-session and expect 403.
Keep Alice’s cookie and add x-role: admin. Observe the vulnerable 200 response and its role-source trace.
Enable Use the server session role. Repeat the forged header request and expect 403.
Test an unknown session with the same forged header, expect 401, then run regressions and record the trust decision.
courses.challenge: Compare an absent session, an unknown session, a real customer session and the real administrator session, with and without x-role: admin.

practice.prompt: Who can choose an x-role request header in this experiment?
practice.explanation: The editor represents a client that controls its own request fields.

practice.prompt: What do the readable lab session ids represent?
practice.explanation: They select known fixtures and intentionally omit a real login lifecycle.

practice.prompt: What isolates the forged-role bug?

options.text: Keeping Alice’s session while adding an admin role header

practice.explanation: The caller remains a customer while the untrusted role claim changes.

questions.prompt: Where should this handler obtain its role?

options.text: The text of the navigation menu

questions.explanation: Authorization should use a trusted identity source rather than caller-controlled claims.

questions.prompt: What should an unknown sid plus x-role: admin produce?
questions.explanation: An untrusted role cannot create a valid authenticated session.

questions.prompt: Would HttpOnly alone fix the forged-role decision?

options.text: Yes; it removes the administrator route
No; the permission check must stop trusting the role header

questions.explanation: HttpOnly concerns script access to cookies, not the provenance of application role claims.

questions.prompt: Which normal behavior must survive the fix?
questions.explanation: Regression testing must preserve permitted administrative access.

questions.prompt: What remains outside this particular experiment?

options.text: A full production login and session lifecycle

questions.explanation: The model exercises role-source trust, not password storage, expiry or token cryptography.

courses.title: 04. Find and repair SQL injection
courses.summary: Observe how a name value changes a query’s logic. Compare a bounded SQL expression evaluator with separate parameter binding.

lessons.title: When data becomes query structure
paragraphs: The intended product search selects a requested name and requires public = yes. The vulnerable handler constructs its WHERE clause by putting the input inside single quotes. A quote inside the input can terminate that literal, allowing the remaining characters to become operators in the query rather than part of a product name.

Lamp and Cable are public products; Prototype is unpublished. A normal Lamp request should return one product. The security rule is not simply that a search succeeds: the response must not expose the unpublished row. The trace shows exactly which expression the model evaluates.
lessons.pitfall: Input validation and a pleasant search interface do not by themselves separate data from SQL syntax.

lessons.title: Reason about the predicate
paragraphs: The guided probe is a closing quote, OR 1=1, and a -- comment. Once concatenated, it makes the condition true for every row and comments out the remainder of the authored query. The extra Prototype result is evidence that the input altered the selection rule. Encode the input as a query value so spaces and special characters reach the handler as intended.

The model tokenizes and evaluates a small SQL WHERE grammar: column or literal equality, inequality, AND, OR and parentheses, with AND taking precedence over OR. It supports a line comment but no database connection, UNION, writes, time delays or arbitrary SQL dialect. An unsupported expression returns 400 and proves only a parser limitation.
lessons.pitfall: A syntax error does not prove that a hidden row was retrieved.

lessons.title: Bind the value separately
paragraphs: With Bind SQL parameters enabled, the query shape remains fixed and the entire input is treated as the name value. The probe then matches no public product, returning 200 with an empty products array. The application can still search for Lamp. The trace now shows a placeholder and a separately recorded bound value.

Parameter binding is the core repair for this value position. When input must choose a column or sort direction, applications need an explicit mapping to permitted identifiers instead of pretending that every part of a SQL statement is a bindable value. This lab models values only.
lessons.pitfall: Blocking one exact probe string does not protect the query from other expressions.

lessons.title: Check more than a single payload
paragraphs: Repeat with a true string comparison, such as OR followed by two equal quoted values, and compare the result. A false expression is a useful negative control. Also search for a literal apostrophe-containing name: a correctly bound value should be accepted as data even if it has no match.

Report the changed query expression and the unauthorized row. After fixing it, include the empty probe response and the intact normal product lookup. Do not describe a 200 empty response as a failed repair: containment is about returned data, not a mandatory error status.
lessons.pitfall: A remediation can safely return 200; inspect the products array rather than judging only the status.

steps: Send /products?name=Lamp and observe one public product.
Load the guided probe and send it. Inspect the constructed SQL and the unpublished Prototype row.
Enable Bind SQL parameters. Repeat the exact probe: expect 200 with an empty products array; Lamp must still work.
Run regressions, try a different true expression and a literal apostrophe, and explain the difference between query structure and bound data.
courses.challenge: Construct a true and a false OR comparison using the supported grammar. Explain their different vulnerable results, then show that both are plain data with parameter binding.

practice.prompt: What makes the probe an injection?
practice.explanation: The string literal is closed and new SQL logic enters the WHERE expression.

practice.prompt: Which returned row establishes the lab’s impact?
practice.explanation: Returning the unpublished row violates the authored public-product condition.

practice.prompt: Which operator binds more tightly in this grammar?

options.text: They are always evaluated in arrival order

practice.explanation: The evaluator groups AND expressions inside the surrounding OR expression.

questions.prompt: What should the fixed handler do with the entire probe?

options.text: Strip only the first quote and run the rest
Treat it as one bound name value

questions.explanation: Binding preserves a fixed query structure while input remains data.

questions.prompt: What is the expected fixed response to the guided probe?
questions.explanation: No public product has the literal injected text as its name.

questions.prompt: Why also test an ordinary name after the repair?

options.text: To confirm legitimate lookup behavior still works
To force the parser to accept UNION

questions.explanation: The repair should preserve allowed product search.

questions.prompt: Does this lab execute arbitrary SQL against a database?

options.text: Yes; it uses the account database
Yes; it sends SQL to an external server
No; it evaluates a documented small expression grammar

questions.explanation: All rows and operations are bounded in-memory teaching data.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with blocking only OR 1=1?

options.text: Equivalent expressions can still change a concatenated query

questions.explanation: Defending one spelling leaves the structural code/data confusion intact.

courses.title: 05. Trace HTML injection and XSS
courses.summary: Follow untrusted search text into an HTML sink. Learn context-aware output encoding and distinguish an injection indicator from demonstrated script execution.

lessons.title: Identify the source and sink
paragraphs: A source is where untrusted data enters a program; a sink is where it is interpreted or used. Here the q query value is the source and the search heading’s HTML text position is the sink. Concatenating the value into markup lets characters such as angle brackets change the intended document structure.

The page displays the generated HTML as inert source text. A structural diagnostic notices markup reaching the sink unchanged. It never executes scripts or event handlers, and it is not a complete HTML parser. This deliberate boundary lets you study the data flow without making the learning application itself vulnerable.
lessons.pitfall: Seeing untrusted markup in the source is evidence of an unsafe sink, not proof that JavaScript ran.

lessons.title: Probe the output context
paragraphs: Begin with the ordinary word Lamp, then send a URL-encoded test. In the vulnerable output, the tag characters survive. The guided example uses an image event-handler attribute to illustrate a common XSS-capable form, but the viewer still treats it as text. Compare the exact input and output rather than waiting for an alert.

Reflected XSS returns request input in an immediate response. Stored XSS retains input for a later viewer, and DOM-based XSS can arise entirely in client-side transformations. This lab demonstrates the reflected HTML text-sink pattern; it does not implement persistence or a real browser exploit.
lessons.pitfall: A filter that recognizes a script tag alone misses other HTML and browser execution contexts.

lessons.title: Encode for the actual context
paragraphs: Enable Encode HTML text output. The handler replaces special characters with HTML entities before placing the value in the heading. A literal less-than sign is now represented as < in the source, so a browser consuming that HTML would treat the search term as text. The original query remains available as data.

HTML text encoding is specific to this sink. An attribute, URL, CSS or JavaScript position has different rules, and intentional rich HTML requires a suitable sanitizer. Prefer framework text rendering when the value is meant to be plain text. A content security policy can provide an additional layer, but is not a substitute for fixing the sink.
lessons.pitfall: Do not apply this text-node encoder blindly to JavaScript source or URL destinations.

lessons.title: Describe the evidence honestly
paragraphs: Compare the complete vulnerable and encoded responses, including ampersands and quotes. Repeating ordinary text verifies that the fix preserves the user’s search term. The lab’s PASS indicates that its fixture encoded the probe; it does not certify every browser context or every route in an application.

Write the source, sink, missing transformation and repair in your report. Explicitly label the observed result as an HTML injection indicator. A real XSS assessment would additionally establish reachable script execution in the relevant browser and policy environment, within the authorized scope.
lessons.pitfall: Do not turn this model’s indicator into a claim that cookies were stolen or code executed.

steps: Send /search?q=Lamp and inspect the generated heading source.
Load the guided markup probe and send it. Find unchanged tag characters in the inert HTML response.
Enable Encode HTML text output and resend. The source should contain < and > instead of executable tag delimiters.
Run regressions, repeat plain text and document the source, text-node sink and absence of actual script execution in this lab.
courses.challenge: Try test, an ampersand and quoted text. Compare raw and encoded output, and explain why the same encoder would not be enough for a JavaScript string sink.

practice.prompt: What is the untrusted source in this lab?
practice.explanation: The caller controls q before it enters the output template.

practice.prompt: Does the lab execute the sample event handler?

options.text: No; generated markup is displayed as inert source
Yes; it runs in the VoltQuest page

practice.explanation: The model reports a structural indicator without inserting untrusted HTML into the DOM.

practice.prompt: Which XSS family does the immediate search response illustrate?
practice.explanation: The input appears directly in the response to the same request.

options.text: Insert the input as raw markup

Trust any value without a script tag

questions.explanation: Plain text should retain its data meaning rather than introduce document structure.

questions.prompt: What does < represent in the encoded source?

options.text: A less-than character treated as text
A command to fetch a file

questions.explanation: The entity represents a text character instead of starting a tag.

questions.prompt: Does a text-node encoder solve every output context?

options.text: Yes; all parsers interpret text identically
Only when the request is POST
No; attribute, URL and script contexts need their own handling

questions.explanation: The safe transformation depends on the interpreter and position receiving the value.

questions.prompt: What can the vulnerable result establish here?

options.text: A script executed on an external host
Untrusted markup reached an HTML sink without encoding
A real visitor’s cookie was stolen

questions.explanation: The fixture intentionally provides no script execution or credential access.

questions.prompt: Why retain the normal Lamp check after patching?

options.text: To verify ordinary text still produces the expected heading
To prove all stored XSS is impossible

questions.explanation: A useful repair keeps legitimate rendering behavior while changing how special characters are handled.

courses.title: 06. Find path traversal in file access
courses.summary: Watch a relative filename escape a public directory. Compare URL decoding, path normalization and a directory containment check.

lessons.title: A filename is an input boundary
paragraphs: The file endpoint intends to serve documents from /public/. The caller supplies name, which is appended to that base path. A path is more than an ordinary label: segments such as .. mean move to the parent directory. A handler that resolves the resulting path without checking its destination can read outside its intended area.

The fixture contains /public/readme.txt, /public/catalog.txt and /private/notes.txt. They are strings in memory, not files on your computer. Access to the private fixture demonstrates an application containment error without exposing an operating system filesystem.
lessons.pitfall: A fixed base prefix before normalization does not guarantee that the final path stays under that base.

lessons.title: Decode, then normalize
paragraphs: Send name=readme.txt and inspect the resolved /public/readme.txt path. Then send ../private/notes.txt, encoding the slashes in the query as needed. URLSearchParams decodes the query once; the path normalizer removes dot segments. Appending the probe to /public/ resolves to /private/notes.txt.

Try images/../../private/notes.txt to see why a probe need not begin with ... The final normalized location matters. Double-encoded percent characters remain literal after this model’s single decoding pass, so they do not magically become another traversal. This behavior is part of the documented model, not a guarantee about every web stack.
lessons.pitfall: Testing the raw spelling before all application decoding can miss what the file lookup actually receives.

lessons.title: Check the resolved boundary
paragraphs: Enable Constrain normalized file paths. The model resolves the path first, then requires it to remain under /public/ with a directory separator. The same private-file probe returns 403. The public manual and public catalog should still return 200.

Real filesystem defenses must account for the actual platform, symlinks and possible changes between validation and opening a file. Often a server-side mapping from permitted document ids to known files is simpler. The lab’s POSIX-style normalizer has no symlinks, drive letters, null bytes or host file operations.
lessons.pitfall: A naive prefix /public would also match /public-other; include the actual directory boundary.

lessons.title: Retest alternate spellings
paragraphs: Use a plain traversal and a nested-directory traversal, then a missing public file. A blocked escape and a missing allowed file are different cases: the former returns 403 and the latter 404 in this model. This distinction helps you inspect the decision sequence.

Document the raw request, decoded value, normalized path and disclosed file content. After the fix, include a public-file success and the denied private-file requests. Keep claims restricted to the fixture because no host filesystem was queried.
lessons.pitfall: A nonexistent file returning 404 does not demonstrate that a traversal was prevented.

steps: Read /files?name=readme.txt and observe /public/readme.txt in the trace.
Send /files?name=..%2Fprivate%2Fnotes.txt and observe the private fixture text.
Enable Constrain normalized file paths. Expect 403 for the same request and 200 for the public manual.
Try images/../../private/notes.txt, run regressions and record the normalized path rather than only the original spelling.
courses.challenge: Compare a normal file, a missing public file, a traversal and a double-encoded traversal. Explain each result using the model’s single decoding pass.

practice.prompt: What does .. mean in a POSIX-style path?
practice.explanation: The normalizer removes one prior segment for each parent traversal.

practice.explanation: The application intends to expose only documents under /public/.

options.text: After the application’s decoding and normalization

practice.explanation: The decision must apply to the same location that the lookup uses.

questions.explanation: The parent segment removes the public directory before private/notes.txt is appended.

questions.prompt: Which fixed result is expected for the private-file probe?
questions.explanation: The resolved location falls outside the permitted directory.

options.text: Only when the path starts with /
No; its file contents are in-memory strings
Yes; relative paths use the working directory

options.text: Symlinks and the actual resolved file location
The color of the download button

options.text: 404 always means the request was authorized

questions.explanation: A known existing private fixture lets you distinguish containment from absence.

courses.title: 07. Protect state changes from forged requests
courses.summary: Model a browser sending a session-bearing request from another origin. Observe an email change and verify origin and session-token defenses.

lessons.title: Identity and user intent differ
paragraphs: An application can receive a valid session cookie without the user intending the action. In a CSRF scenario, an attacker causes a browser to submit a request to a site where the victim is authenticated. Whether cookies are attached depends on browser context and cookie policy; a session-bearing request alone does not demonstrate the user’s intent.

The lab lets you explicitly supply a demo cookie and Origin value. It models the server’s decision after receipt. It does not emulate browser cookie attachment, SameSite behavior, CORS preflights or navigation. The JSON body editor represents parsed fields, which a real handler might receive from a form.
lessons.pitfall: CORS is not a universal CSRF defense: preventing response reads does not necessarily prevent a state-changing request.

lessons.title: Observe a state change
paragraphs: The normal email update uses Alice’s session, Origin https://shop.vq.test, and body fields email and csrf with the value csrf-alice. Send it and inspect both previous and new email. Then keep the session, use https://other.vq.test as Origin and remove the token field.

With the defense disabled, the server still changes the email. The impact is the mutation visible in the fixture, not just a successful response. The attacker in a real scenario need not be able to read the response for the unwanted action to matter.
lessons.pitfall: A read-only request is not a sufficient demonstration of this state-change vulnerability.

lessons.title: Bind the request to its session
paragraphs: Enable Validate origin and CSRF token. The handler now requires the exact expected origin and the token associated with the authenticated session. A token from Bob’s session does not authorize Alice’s request. Failed checks occur before the account email is updated.

The predictable csrf-alice value is a fixture chosen for inspection. Real tokens must have appropriate unpredictability and session binding, and should be handled by a framework’s established protection. The lab uses a strict origin policy; a real application must deliberately handle legitimate contexts where an Origin header is unavailable.
lessons.pitfall: A nonempty token is not enough; compare it to the token bound to the current session.

lessons.title: Test each check independently
paragraphs: Try a correct origin without a token, a wrong origin with the right token, and the right origin with another user’s token. Each should fail in the patched fixture. Then repeat the legitimate update to ensure the defense does not block the intended form.

Changing defenses resets fixture accounts so an earlier successful mutation cannot contaminate the retest. Regression checks also start fresh. In your report, distinguish the request context, the missing check, the observed mutation and the browser behaviors this server-side model does not simulate.
lessons.pitfall: Do not treat a token displayed in this lab as a production secret or as evidence that real browsers send the same request.

steps: Send the normal POST /account/email request and inspect the previous and new email.
Load the cross-origin probe: Alice’s cookie remains, Origin is other.vq.test and csrf is absent. Observe the unwanted update.
Enable Validate origin and CSRF token. Repeat the probe and expect 403 with the fixture email unchanged.
Try csrf-bob with Alice’s session, run regressions, then show a legitimate update still succeeds.
courses.challenge: Test all four combinations of matching/mismatching origin and matching/missing token. Include the account email before and after each attempt.

options.text: No; the unwanted mutation can be sufficient
Yes; otherwise the request cannot be sent

options.text: The token bound to Alice’s session

options.text: No; it models the handler after receiving explicit fields

courses.title: 08. Constrain server-side URL destinations
courses.summary: Investigate a preview feature that can reach an internal service fixture. Learn parsed URL allowlists and the limits of a static network model.

lessons.title: The server becomes a requester
paragraphs: A URL preview feature accepts a destination from a user and retrieves content on their behalf. The server may be able to reach services unavailable to an ordinary visitor. If the destination is not constrained, a public feature can cross into that internal network boundary. This is the central trust problem behind SSRF.

VoltShop has two known service fixtures: a public news article and an internal inventory status. The model uses a parsed URL to select a local object. It has no DNS resolution, socket, fetch call or proxy. An unfamiliar destination therefore returns a fixture error rather than contacting a network.
lessons.pitfall: An internal-looking URL in a report is not evidence of SSRF unless the server-side feature actually returns or causes a relevant effect.

lessons.title: Change the destination
paragraphs: Send /preview with the public article URL and note the title. Change only the url query value to http://inventory.internal/status. With the defense off, the response contains internal inventory data. This demonstrates that the public preview accepts a destination outside its intended service boundary.

The destination is encoded inside an outer query string. Inspect the decoded URL and parsed origin in the trace. The browser address bar is still the VoltQuest lab; the nested URL is input to the teaching handler. This distinction makes the request chain easier to explain.
lessons.pitfall: Do not confuse the page you are viewing with the destination supplied to a server-side feature.

lessons.title: Validate the parsed origin
paragraphs: Enable Allow only the public news origin. The handler permits https://news.vq.test with no URL credentials and rejects the internal destination. It compares the parsed origin, including scheme and port semantics, rather than searching the original string for a familiar hostname.

A URL can contain a username before @. In https://news.vq.test@inventory.internal/status, the familiar text is a username and the host is inventory.internal. The parsed URL check rejects it. The lab also refuses unfamiliar fixture paths rather than inventing a response.
lessons.pitfall: A substring check can be fooled by userinfo or lookalike hostnames.

lessons.title: Plan the real-world retest
paragraphs: Real outbound request controls need to consider DNS resolution, address ranges, redirects, protocol restrictions and egress policy. An allowed hostname can resolve unexpectedly, and a redirect can change the destination. This static fixture has no redirects or DNS, so passing its checks cannot establish those properties.

Report the public feature, controlled destination, returned internal fields and the exact allowlist repair. Verify that the normal article remains accessible. Include the hostname-as-username probe to show why structured URL parsing matters, while keeping real network claims outside the observed evidence.
lessons.pitfall: An origin allowlist tested against static objects is not a complete production SSRF defense.

steps: Send the normal preview request and confirm the public article response.
Change the encoded destination to http://inventory.internal/status. Observe internal stock data.
Enable Allow only the public news origin and expect 403 for the internal destination, with the public article still working.
Test https://news.vq.test@inventory.internal/status, run regressions and explain the parsed host and the model’s DNS/redirect limits.
courses.challenge: Compare the permitted origin, a different port, a lookalike hostname and a username-before-@ URL. Use the parsed origin to explain each rejection.

courses.title: 09. Find mass assignment and privilege changes
courses.summary: Add an unexpected profile field and follow its effect into an administrator route. Repair the update schema and test the complete sequence.

lessons.title: Writable fields are a policy
paragraphs: A profile form may intend to update only a display name, while the server’s user object also contains a role. If a handler copies caller-supplied fields into that object, a field absent from the visible form may still become writable. The allowed update shape is a server-side policy, not a consequence of which inputs the UI shows.

The fixture accepts a name update. In vulnerable mode it also copies a supplied role. These are explicit modeled assignments; the engine never merges arbitrary objects into application prototypes. The lesson concerns permission over data fields, rather than prototype pollution or arbitrary code execution.
lessons.pitfall: Hiding role from the profile form does not make it immutable on the server.

lessons.title: Extend the normal JSON body
paragraphs: First PATCH /profile as Alice with a name field and inspect the updated profile. Then add role: admin to the same JSON body. The vulnerable response shows that Alice’s server-side role changed. Unlike the forged header lesson, this changes the trusted record itself and can affect later requests.

Follow with GET /admin using only sid=alice-session. The administrator handler may correctly trust the server session role and still grant access, because another handler already corrupted that role. This chain separates the initial field-write bug from the downstream permission decision.
lessons.pitfall: A secure read handler cannot repair an earlier unauthorized write to the identity data it trusts.

lessons.title: Reject fields outside the update schema
paragraphs: Enable Allow only editable profile fields. The model now rejects an update containing anything other than name before changing the user record. The name-only update should succeed. Rejecting the whole unexpected shape makes the result easy to observe and avoids a partial mutation before validation completes.

A production design can use an explicit update object or a dedicated data-transfer schema and assign only permitted fields. Administrative role changes should have their own permission checks and workflow. This fixture uses a small allowlist and does not provide a general role-management API.
lessons.pitfall: A blocklist of known sensitive keys can miss a sensitive field added later.

lessons.title: Reset state before verifying the chain
paragraphs: A role already changed by an earlier request will not automatically become safe because the profile handler is patched. The lab resets fixture data when a defense changes, and the regression runner uses fresh state. From a clean Alice session, replay the forbidden profile update and the administrator read.

The patched update should return 400 and the following admin read 403. Also submit a valid name-only update and verify that it remains available. Your report should include both exchanges from the vulnerable chain, the initial state and the corresponding clean-state retest.
lessons.pitfall: A retest using an already promoted account does not isolate whether the field-write fix works.

steps: Send a normal name-only PATCH /profile using Alice’s cookie.
Add role: admin, send the request, then GET /admin with the same cookie and no role header. Observe the 200 dashboard.
Enable Allow only editable profile fields; the fixture accounts reset. The same PATCH must return 400.
GET /admin now returns 403 for Alice. Run regressions and include a successful name-only update in your report.
courses.challenge: Show that Use the server session role can remain enabled while the mass-assignment chain succeeds. Explain which handler must be repaired and why a clean fixture matters.

courses.title: 10. Investigate and harden VoltShop
courses.summary: Combine request mapping, independent findings, a privilege-change chain and regression evidence into one reproducible investigation report.

lessons.title: Set the scope and establish controls
paragraphs: The capstone enables three weaknesses together: public diagnostic exposure, missing order ownership checks and writable profile roles. The other modeled defenses begin enabled. Your scope is the local VoltShop fixture and its listed endpoints. Establish normal requests for service health, customer order access and profile updates before investigating unusual behavior.

Use the route map to plan a small test matrix. Record the actor and object for every request, and keep normal traffic alongside probes. A hypothesis should name a boundary: anonymous versus operator data, Alice versus Bob’s record, or customer-editable versus administrator-only fields.
lessons.pitfall: Running a list of payloads without an expected rule makes results difficult to interpret.

lessons.title: Separate independent issues from a chain
paragraphs: Read /debug anonymously and document the internal structure disclosure. Read Bob’s order as Alice to establish an independent ownership failure. Then add a role field to Alice’s profile update and use the same session to read /admin. The last two requests form one privilege-change chain rooted in the unauthorized profile write.

Do not count the successful admin read as a second independent vulnerability when its cause is the changed role. The administrator handler’s trusted-role check is enabled. Explain how each request changes state or exposes data, and identify the earliest missing control that makes each result possible.
lessons.pitfall: Counting every downstream symptom as a separate root cause can overstate an investigation.

lessons.title: Repair and run the full matrix
paragraphs: Enable all three missing controls. Every defense change starts the shop fixtures fresh while leaving the request history available as captured evidence. Replay the probes and confirm 404 for debug, 403 for Alice reading Bob’s order, and 400 then 403 for the profile-to-admin chain.

Run the full regression matrix. It also exercises the other labs’ normal requests and alternate probes, so an accidentally disabled defense remains visible. A passing result belongs to the exact current defense settings. Editing those settings invalidates the displayed verification until you run it again.
lessons.pitfall: An old green result does not describe a newly changed configuration.

lessons.title: Write a bounded, useful report
paragraphs: For each root cause, include the affected endpoint, fixture identity, initial state, exact steps, expected behavior, observed evidence, impact and fix. Include the retest with both rejected probes and normal requests. The report export contains captured request/response history and the latest regression output, together with your notes.

Describe uncertainty and model limits explicitly: SQL is a small grammar, HTML output is inert, file and service lookups use fixtures, and browser session transport is not emulated. The course exam tests reasoning; it is separate from your lab evidence and grants no campaign XP or professional certification.
lessons.pitfall: Passing these local exercises does not establish that a real production application is secure.

steps: Send the normal health request, then map order and profile behavior using the route map and demo sessions.
Reproduce the anonymous debug leak and Alice-to-Bob order read. Add role: admin to Alice’s profile, then confirm her /admin access.
Enable Disable public debug data, Check order ownership and Allow only editable profile fields. Replay each finding from fresh fixture state.
Run the full regression matrix, write one report entry per root cause and export the captured investigation report before taking the exam.
courses.challenge: Produce three findings with exact evidence, distinguish the profile-to-admin chain from the independent order leak, and deliver a passing full regression report that preserves normal shop operations.
